items.item: A stage's boundary is determined by dependency type between RDDs/DataFrames in the lineage graph, never by the number of operators chained — an arbitrarily long narrow chain still costs one stage.

at.step: Reveal: a narrow chain, one stage

items.item: map, filter and select are canonical narrow operations; groupBy, join (against non-co-partitioned inputs) and repartition are canonical wide operations.

items.item: A join can actually be narrow if both sides are already partitioned identically (hash- or range-co-partitioned) — this topic names the general rule and defers the co-partitioned exception to this chapter's own bucketing topic (§7.2).

at.out: bucketing and storage-partitioned joins, §7.2's own topic

items.item: Each independent wide dependency in a plan cuts its own stage boundary; stage count is one plus the number of shuffles, not a fixed property of the job or capped at some maximum.

items.item: count() as an action always includes its own final single-partition merge stage, even over an otherwise purely narrow chain, which is why this topic's own measurements use collect() to isolate the narrow/wide distinction cleanly.

at.out: an examples.py methodology note, not itself a syllabus clause; disclosed in FACT-CHECK.md

items.item: A stage boundary is a materialisation point (shuffle output written so the next stage can read it), not merely a lineage split — the DAG itself has no 'breaks', only a continuous dependency graph the scheduler cuts at specific points.

at.step: Reveal: why the cut happens there

items.item: The DAGScheduler walks the lineage graph backward from the final RDD to build the DAG of stages, rather than scheduling forward from the sources — a detail the original paper states explicitly.

Stage-map output materialisation (writing shuffle files to disk on the nodes holding the producing partitions) is what makes a wide dependency's recovery cost higher than a narrow one's: a lost node can force recomputation of an entire ancestor stage, not just the lost partitions.

items.item: A `union` between two RDDs is narrow (each child partition depends on exactly one parent partition from one of the two inputs), despite combining two different RDDs — narrowness is about per-partition dependency count, not about how many RDDs are involved.

at.out: named only as a boundary case strengthening the narrow/wide definition; not separately measured in this topic's examples.py

items.item: Catalyst's physical plan represents a wide dependency's cut point as an explicit Exchange node; this topic's own examples.py greps queryExecution().toString() for that exact string as its evidence, matching how a real engineer would confirm a shuffle from EXPLAIN output.
